native_language: Coptic (liturgical only since ~17th century); Arabic (daily life)
native_script: Coptic alphabet — modified Greek script with 7 additional characters from Demotic Egyptian; oldest continuous Christian liturgical script in the world
current_script: Arabic for all daily life; Coptic used only in church liturgy — a language community that has lost its spoken language but preserved its written sacred form
arabization_status: Complete in spoken life — Coptic became extinct as a daily spoken language by approximately the 17th century; survives only in liturgy and is being revived by diaspora communities; Egypt's indigenous language before Arabic, before Islam, and before Christianity
language_vitality: Coptic language: dormant (liturgical only); revival efforts in diaspora, especially USA and Australia
human_scale_fact: The Coptic Church is the oldest continuously operating Christian institution in Africa — founded before Rome adopted Christianity, before the New Testament was fully assembled, before the Council of Nicaea defined the Christian creed. The word 'Copt' simply means 'Egyptian' — it is what Egyptians called themselves before the Arab conquest. When Copts are persecuted in Egypt, they are being persecuted in the land their ancestors have called home for 5,000 years. Egypt's constitution guarantees freedom of religion but church construction requires presidential approval — a process that can take decades. There are governorates in Upper Egypt where there is not a single licensed church for hundreds of thousands of Christians.
key_quote: We are not a minority in Egypt. We are Egypt. Our ancestors built the pyramids, translated the Bible into Greek, and gave the world monasticism. We were here before Islam. We will be here after.
israel_connection: ~130,000 Arab Christians (largely Melkite and Greek Orthodox but also some Coptic) are full Israeli citizens; Israel-Egypt peace treaty (1979) enables Coptic pilgrimages to Sinai sites including St. Catherine's Monastery; relations generally positive

name: Maronite Catholic Church
subtitle: Lebanon's Christians — constitutionally entrenched, demographically squeezed
note_on_numbers: Lebanese census is deliberately not conducted — last official census was 1932 under French Mandate. All population figures are estimates. Christian share of Lebanese population has fallen from ~55% (1932) to estimated 30–35% today.

Today — estimated ~20% of Lebanese citizens; diaspora larger than homeland population

key_destruction_events.event: Druze-Maronite sectarian massacres in Mount Lebanon — 10,000 killed; France sends troops; reshapes Lebanese identity politics for 150 years
Lebanese Civil War begins — 15 years of conflict kill 120,000; Maronite militias (Phalange, South Lebanon Army) commit and suffer atrocities

native_language: Arabic (daily life); Syriac (liturgy — they are ethnically Syriac in origin)
native_script: Arabic script for daily life; Syriac Estrangela for liturgy; historically used Garshuni (Arabic text written in Syriac script)
current_script: Arabic; liturgical Syriac maintained; Garshuni script historically preserved Maronite identity when Arabic script would have meant Islamic cultural absorption
arabization_status: Largely Arabized in language; Maronites maintain distinct identity through church, French cultural influence, and diaspora connections; Lebanon's French-language education system historically a Maronite institution
language_vitality: Syriac liturgical language: maintained in church; spoken Syriac/Aramaic: extinct among Lebanese Maronites for centuries
human_scale_fact: Lebanon is the only Arab country where a Christian must constitutionally be head of state — the President of Lebanon must be a Maronite Christian, the Prime Minister a Sunni Muslim, the Speaker of Parliament a Shia Muslim. This 1943 National Pact was based on the 1932 French census showing a Christian majority. No census has been conducted since — because the results would require renegotiating the entire political system. Meanwhile Lebanese Christians are the most educated and economically productive emigrant community in Latin America: Brazil alone has more people of Lebanese Christian origin (~7–10 million) than all of Lebanon.
key_quote: We invented Lebanon. The idea that Arabs and Christians could coexist in one country — we built that. And now they are dismantling it around us, piece by piece.
israel_connection: Complex — Maronite South Lebanon Army (SLA) allied with Israel during civil war; Major Saad Haddad's forces worked with IDF; SLA members and families (~6,000) fled to Israel after 2000 Israeli withdrawal; small Maronite village of Ghajar on Israel-Lebanon border straddles the line

native_language: Neo-Aramaic (Sureth/Chaldean for Chaldean Catholics; Assyrian Neo-Aramaic for Church of the East) — the closest living languages to Biblical Aramaic
native_script: Syriac script — East Syriac style (Madnhaya) for Church of the East; West Syriac (Serto) for some Chaldean; one of the oldest continuously used alphabets
current_script: Arabic imposed for all civil purposes; Syriac maintained in church, school, and diaspora community life; Neo-Aramaic increasingly written in modified Latin script in diaspora
arabization_status: Severe and ongoing — Nineveh Plains Arabized under Saddam with Kurdish and Arab settlement replacing Christian villages; Assyrian place names replaced; after ISIS, Christian-owned property distributed to Arab and Kurdish settlers; return complicated by property disputes
language_vitality: Chaldean Neo-Aramaic (Sureth): endangered — ~300,000 speakers, majority in diaspora. Assyrian Neo-Aramaic: endangered — ~500,000 speakers. Both losing child speakers rapidly in diaspora.
human_scale_fact: The Chaldean Catholic and Assyrian churches trace their origins to the earliest Christian mission — tradition holds that St. Thomas the Apostle evangelized Mesopotamia and Mar Addai (Thaddaeus) founded the church in Edessa. Their liturgical language, Syriac, is a dialect of Aramaic — the language Jesus spoke. When an elderly Chaldean woman in Dearborn, Michigan recites the Lord's Prayer in Syriac, she is speaking words in the same language they were first spoken. Iraq's Christian population was 1.5 million in 2003. In 20 years of church bombings, kidnappings, ISIS ultimatums, and quiet daily persecution, it has fallen below 250,000. The Nineveh Plains — where Assyrians have lived continuously for 7,000 years — was emptied in 72 hours in August 2014.
key_quote: They painted the letter N on our doors. N for Nasrani — Christian. The same thing the Nazis did with the Star of David. And the world watched.
key_quote_attribution: Chaldean Catholic priest, formerly of Mosul, now in Detroit, 2015
israel_connection: Small Assyrian community in Israel; Aramaic-speaking Christians in the village of Jish (Gush Halav) in Galilee maintain liturgical Aramaic; Israel one of few states to formally name the Seyfo as genocide

native_language: Arabic (Greek Orthodox, Melkite); Syriac/Aramaic (Syriac Orthodox liturgy); Greek (historical Greek Orthodox liturgy, now largely Arabic)
native_script: Arabic script (daily life and most liturgy); Syriac script (Syriac Orthodox liturgy — Serto style); Greek alphabet (historical)
current_script: Arabic universally; Syriac maintained in Syriac Orthodox monasteries and diaspora; Greek retained only in Ecumenical Patriarchate context
arabization_status: Greek Orthodox of Antioch adopted Arabic liturgy centuries ago — arguably the most successfully Arabized Christian community; their identity is Arab-Christian not Greek; Syriac Orthodox have maintained Aramaic liturgy against Arabization pressure
language_vitality: Aramaic (Maaloula dialect, the last spoken western Aramaic): critically endangered — fewer than 15,000 speakers in the world; Syriac liturgical: maintained; Arabic: dominant
human_scale_fact: Antioch — modern Antakya in Turkey — is where followers of Jesus were first called 'Christians.' The city was one of the greatest in the Roman Empire and the base for Paul's missionary journeys. The Patriarchate of Antioch, which oversees the Greek Orthodox and Syriac Orthodox churches of Syria and Lebanon, is one of the five original patriarchates of Christianity — older than the Roman Catholic Church's claims of supremacy, older than Constantinople, older than Islam by 600 years. The village of Maaloula, 50 km from Damascus, is one of the last places on earth where Western Aramaic — the language Jesus spoke — is still used in daily life. Al-Nusra Front fighters stormed it in 2013. Two senior bishops of the Greek Orthodox Church of Antioch were kidnapped in Aleppo in 2013. Their fate remains unknown.
key_quote: Antioch was Christian before Rome was Christian. We did not come here from somewhere else. We are from here. The question is whether 'here' will still exist for us.
israel_connection: Greek Orthodox Patriarchate of Jerusalem (separate from Antioch) is a major landholder in Israel and the Palestinian territories; Israeli Arab Christians are largely Melkite and Greek Orthodox; Aramaic-speaking village of Gush Halav in Galilee; complex property disputes between Patriarchate and Israeli government
